name: desire for safety
description: A desire to get out of a situation of perceived bodily or social danger. This desire is the result of fear or anxiety.
perceptions: Your body or an important social identity are threatened.
results: desire to remove or escape the perceived threat

guidance.description: Remaining composed enough to respond appropriately to danger can take courage.

variations.name: desire to escape danger
variations.description: Your physical safety is threatened when your body is in danger. If someone is perceived as causing this threat, it can come with anger.
results: desire to remove or escape the perceived threat

variations.name: desire to escape social threat
variations.description: Your social safety is threatened when your status and reputation are perceived as being attacked. This may come with anger or other negative social experiences like shame.
perceptions: An important social identity is threatened.
results: desire to remove or escape the perceived threat

commentaries.quote: This is the flight-freeze-flight reaction. 'Safety' could be thought of as a kind of 'existential comfort' that is often prioritized over physical comfort. This also covers social dangers because we're aware of how much we depend on others, we often link 'social comfort' and 'existential comfort'.

Even though we may not always be aware of danger on a cognitive level, on a neurophysiological level, our body has already started a sequence of neural processes that would facilitate adaptive defense behaviors such as fight, flight or freeze.
commentaries.attribution: Stephen W. Porges in 'The Polyvagal Theory: Neurophysiological Foundations of Emotions, Attachment, Communication, and Self-Regulation'

commentaries.quote: My fight-or-flight response was currently telling me to get the hell outta there. Except that my fight-or-flight response had a third, less-evolved option called deer-in-the-headlights.
